title: How to Use a Spiralizer for Spiralized Sweet Potato
meta_description: Learn step‑by‑step how to master a spiralizer for spiralized sweet potato, from prep to cooking tips, and discover the best vegetable spiralizer for low‑carb me
html:
Spiralizing sweet potatoes is a game‑changer for low‑carb dinners, breakfast bowls, and even kid‑friendly fries. Using a spiralizer for spiralized sweet potato adds texture, flavor, and a splash of color to any plate. Below is a practical guide that walks you through cleaning, cutting, and cooking sweet potato ribbons, plus a few tricks to keep them from turning mushy.

Choosing the Right Spiralizer for Sweet Potato

Sweet potatoes are denser than zucchini or carrots, so you’ll want a sturdy model. Handheld options work for occasional use, but a countertop unit—like the Vegetable Spiralizer—offers more leverage and a smoother feed. Look for a spiralizer with a sharp stainless‑steel blade and an adjustable crank; these features reduce the effort needed to push the sweet potato through and produce even, consistent strands.

Prep: Getting Your Sweet Potato Ready

Before you even touch the spiralizer, give the sweet potato a quick prep:

  1. Wash and dry. Scrub the skin under running water. You can leave the skin on for extra fiber, but peel it if you prefer a smoother noodle.
  2. Trim the ends. Cut off about a half‑inch from both ends to create flat surfaces for the spiralizer’s feed tube.
  3. Cut to length. Most countertop spiralizers accept pieces up to 12 inches long. If your sweet potato is longer, slice it into manageable sections.

Because sweet potatoes are hard, it helps to microwave them for 2–3 minutes or blanch them in boiling water for 30 seconds. This softens the flesh just enough to make spiraling easier without cooking them fully.

How to Use a Spiralizer for Spiralized Sweet Potato

With your Vegetable Spiralizer set up on a stable countertop, follow these steps:

  • Secure the blade. Make sure the blade is locked in place and that the safety guard is engaged.
  • Insert the sweet potato. Feed the trimmed end into the feed tube. Use the crank handle to turn the potato slowly; the blade will slice it into ribbons as it moves.
  • Collect the strands. The spiralizer’s basket catches the noodles. If you’re using a handheld model, guide the strands onto a plate as they fall.
  • Trim excess. Once you’ve finished one piece, use kitchen scissors to cut any remaining stub that didn’t fit the tube.

For a finer noodle, switch to a smaller blade size if your spiralizer offers multiple options. A thicker cut works well for stir‑fries and baked dishes, while a thin cut mimics traditional pasta.

Cooking Tips for Sweet Potato Noodles

Spiralized sweet potatoes hold up well to both quick sautéing and longer baking. Here are three reliable methods:

  1. Sauté. Heat 1‑2 tbsp of olive oil in a skillet over medium‑high heat. Add the noodles, toss for 3‑4 minutes, and season with salt, pepper, and a pinch of smoked paprika. They’ll be tender‑crisp, perfect for a low‑carb pasta substitute.
  2. Roast. Spread the ribbons on a parchment‑lined baking sheet, drizzle with a little oil, and bake at 425°F for 15‑20 minutes, turning halfway. The edges caramelize, giving you sweet‑potato fries with a noodle shape.
  3. Steam. Place the noodles in a steamer basket over simmering water for 5‑6 minutes. This method keeps them bright and retains nutrients, ideal for a gentle side dish or a base for a warm salad.

Regardless of the method, do not over‑cook. Sweet potato noodles can become gummy if left too long.

Storing and Reusing Spiralized Sweet Potato

If you’ve made a batch ahead of time, store the dry noodles in an airtight container lined with a paper towel. They’ll keep in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, blanch the noodles for 1 minute, cool them in an ice bath, then freeze in zip‑top bags. When you’re ready to use them, thaw in the fridge and give them a quick sauté or steam.

Creative Recipes to Try

Now that you’ve mastered the spiralizer for spiralized sweet potato, experiment with these simple recipes:

  • Sweet Potato Pesto Pasta. Toss sautéed noodles with basil pesto, toasted pine nuts, and grated Parmesan.
  • Spicy Sweet Potato Stir‑Fry. Combine noodles with bell peppers, snap peas, garlic, ginger, and a splash of soy‑sriracha sauce.
  • Breakfast Sweet Potato Hash. Roast the noodles with onions, mushrooms, and a fried egg on top.

These dishes showcase the versatility of sweet potato ribbons and keep meals exciting without relying on grain‑based pasta.

FAQ

Can I use a handheld spiralizer for sweet potatoes?

Yes, but a handheld model requires more force and may produce uneven strands. For frequent use, a countertop unit like the Vegetable Spiralizer provides smoother, more consistent results.

Do I need to peel sweet potatoes before spiraling?

Peeling is optional. The skin adds fiber and a rustic look, but if you prefer a smoother texture or plan to use the noodles in a delicate sauce, peel them first.

What’s the best way to prevent sweet potato noodles from sticking together?

After spiraling, toss the noodles lightly with a tablespoon of oil or a splash of lemon juice. Storing them with a paper towel in the container also absorbs excess moisture that can cause clumping.
